MH 370 Wreckage

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Two South Africans have recently found debris which could turn out to be from the missing Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 - could the finds finally bring closure to the families of the 239 victims?

Summary:
In December 2015, Liam Lotter, an 18 year old South African, found a piece of aeroplane debris floating off the coast of Mozambique where he was on holiday with his family. Then in March this year Neels Kruger found another piece in Mossel Bay and has been sent to Australia for testing. These two parts brings the total possible finds to 4 pieces. If confirmed, could these be parts help solve the mystery that is Flight MH370?

Further information:
Our story will recap the original incident with victims, the rescue teams and the all efforts to recover any of the wreckage. Both South African case studies have agreed to speak to us. We'll be speaking to experts in the aviation industry to be better understand what went wrong, and why in today's techno age we still don't know what happened to the 239 people aboard. Conspiracy theorist and self-proclaimed MH370 investigator Blaine Gibson has been around the world trying to locate the missing flight. Last year he found a confirmed piece (the second), also off of the coast of African - in Mozambique. We've approached him for an interview, if he does not return contact we've got his websites, video's and photo's of him conducting his investigations. He is one of many "conspiracy theorists" and has compiled a list of facts and questions. We do have footage of the man in the reunion islands who found a confirmed piece last year, he was the first to do so, and since then the investigations have primarily been focused on the South Indian Ocean.

Lastly, we will be speaking to an expert to the South African weather services who can explain flo-patterns in the ocean and why the debris is landing on Southern Africa's shores. The South African Civil Aviation authority is providing us with general footage that can be used for the story, as well as an interview with an air traffic control expert.

Extra Budget Items:
We are going to be using extra footage from Getty/Gallo/AFP.

Press Release:


MH 370
Aircraft debris found off the coasts of Mozambique and Mossel Bay may at long last reveal what really happened to Malaysian Airlines Flight MH370. Investigators are hoping these latest fragments will provide fresh clues into what led to the plane’s sinister disappearance over two years ago. Could we be on the brink of solving the air crash mystery of the century and bringing closure to the relatives of the 227 passengers and 12 crew members who vanished with the plane?


Script:


Mh370 Wreckage
Script 1 April 2016

Voice
It’s 12:41 am local time on the 8th of March 2014. Malaysian Airlines Flight MH370 has just departed Kuala Lumpur International Airport en route to Beijing. Leveling out at 35 000 feet, everything on board the flight seems perfectly normal.

Sound Up Radio Comm
Tower: Malaysian Three Seven Zero climb flight level three five zero.

MH370: Flight level three five zero Malaysian Three Seven Zero. Malaysian Three Seven Zero maintaining level three five zero.

Voice
On board are 227 passengers, mostly Chinese nationals, and 12 crewmembers. 40 minutes into the flight, as MH 370 is about to leave Malaysian Airspace and enter Vietnamese airspace, air traffic control directs the flight to contact their counterparts in Ho Chi Min City. It will be the last time anyone hears from the doomed Boeing 777.

Sound Up Radio Comm
Tower: Malaysian Three Seven Zero contact Ho Chi Min 120 decimal 9. Good night.

MH370: Good night Malaysian Three Seven Zero

Link Devi
In a time where a simple cell phone application like Whatsapp can send your exact location to anybody in the world, how is it that a Boeing 777 weighing 290 tons can simply disappear off the face of the earth.

Sound Up Jeoffrey Matshoba
It is indeed a mystery, and there could be several factors that could be attributed to that, and there are many.

Voice
Jeoffrey Matshoba is a senior executive of Air Trafic Management and Planning at Air Traffic and Navigation Services. ATNS is responsible for managing all air traffic within South African airspace.

Sound Up Jeoffrey
It could be technical failures of the system on board the aircraft, it could be unlawful interference, and it could be the pilot error, that is your human factor, and it could be that the system was tampered with by whoever.

Voice
Mh370’s final good night took place at 01:19 local time. What happened next would lead to one of the most inexplicable aircraft disasters of modern times. Several of the plane’s key communications and tracking systems were either turned off or malfunctioned and it disappeared from air traffic controllers’ radar screens at 01:22am. At the same time the flight veered completely off course and traveled back over the Malaysian peninsula where it was picked up by Malaysian military radar. British satellite data shows the flight continued south for at least another 7 hours until 08:19 the next morning. After that, having run out of fuel and with nowhere to land, it is assumed the flight crashed somewhere in the southern Indian Ocean. Two years later MH370 is still missing.

Link Devi
But now, thousands of kilometers from the suspected crash site, debris possibly from flight MH 370, has been washing up along the Southern African Coastline.

Sound Up Liam Lötter
It looked like it had just been washed up and it was just lying there. Sort of, it had this curve to it, like this, and the paint was on the bottom, so we just saw this white on the inside. Then when we turned it over then you could see the serial number and all the honeycomb and all of that.

Voice
Eighteen-year-old Liam Lötter from Wartburg in Kwazulu Natal was on holiday in Mozambique in December 2015 when he, his cousin and his brother spotted a strange object on the beach near Guinjata Bay.

Sound Up Liam
And my cousin immediately told me: “Hey this is from an airplane.” And he knew what he was looking at, and he said: “There’s rivets, there’s a serial number, it’s the honeycomb.” And he just put it all together and said” ja it’s part of an aeroplane.”

Voice
Liam suspected the part could be from MH370 and took it home with him.

Sound Up Liam
So I picked this thing up and carted it all the way to the house, and everyone was like: “ No you’re mad. You’ve brought rubbish up to the house, you’re mad, you crazy thing, you fool.”

Voice
Mom Candace admits she was initially skeptical of Liam’s find.

Sound Up Candace Lötter
The kids got back from the beach and brought this piece of “rubbish” up, and Liam said he’s taking it home it could be from the Malaysian airline and I said: ”ugh its just a piece of rubbish” and it was full of sand and water logged and I just couldn’t see that this was going to hang around the holiday home for another few days and then get taken home.

Voice
But the family did bring the piece of debris back to South Africa with them, where it was nearly forgotten about until Candace saw an article on another piece of debris found in Mozambique by American adventurer Blaine Gibson.

Sound Up Candace
We took it out, we looked at it, we compared it to the picture of Blaine Gibson’s in the newspaper.

Sound Up Liam
And everything matched, the colours, the honeycomb, the rivet holes, everything was there.

Voice
The first, and to date only confirmed piece of debris from MH 370 to be found washed up on the shores of Reunion Island in the Indian ocean on the 29th of July last year. It was spotted by resident Johnny Begg as he was searching for a stone to crush chilies with.

Sound Up Johnny
That’s when I saw it. I went down to the water to see if it was plane debris, and I could see that it was by the rounded shape. I could see that there were screws on it that weren’t rusty, and I could see that there were barnacles on it. Then I looked at the material itself and I concluded that it must be plane debris.

Voice
Malaysian officials confirmed the object to be a flaperon from a Boeing 777 aircraft on the 2nd of August last year, and three days later the Malaysian Prime Minister confirmed it was from Flight Mh 370.

Sound Up Johnny
It is sad for everyone. I had no family on that plane, but those people are now my family. I feel something for them.

Voice
The latest discovery of possible MH 370 debris was found just two weeks ago on the 21st of March by South African archeologist Neels Kruger. While on holiday in Mosselbay, Neels spotted a strange object lying in the sand near the Klein Brak River.

Sound Up Neels
As an archeologist I always pick up stuff, and I examine stuff and I’m always curious about things that I see on the ground. But with this object I immediately sensed that this is kind of a high tech object. It’s not like regular marine debris or refuse.

Voice
Having followed the MH370 tragedy closely, Neels immediately suspected he may have found a part of the doomed airplane when he picked up the object and recognized the familiar logo of engine manufacturer Rolls Royce imprinted on it.

Sound Up Neels
That’s when you know the chills just ran down my spine because I immediately recognized that this is from an aircraft. And probably from a large aircraft.

Voice
Both Neels and Liam’s finds were collected by the South African Civil aviation authorities and sent on to Australia, which has spearheaded the hunt for Mh370 ever since the search area moved to the southern Indian Ocean.

Link Devi
These finds could have huge implications, forensic investigations are already being conducted on the debris, including an analysis on microscopic marine life, which could shed some light on where exactly in the ocean the crash occurred.

Sound Up Candace
Joe Hattley’s first email to me was you no longer touch it. It’s now a piece of evidence, it will have minute traces on it that mean nothing to you but means a lot to them, so ja we were very careful with it from then on.

Sound Up Neels
I’m not an expert but from what I understand they can use that to trace back that object to a certain location in the ocean you know where you will then find these kind of micro species of marine biology.

Voice
In a statement by the Australian minister for infrastucture and transport Darren Chester, he confirmed “the debris found in Mozambique is almost certainly from MH370.”

Sound Up Candace
Devi: How did you feel knowing that sitting here in your shed in Wartburg was a piece that could solve an international mystery?

Candace: It’s just… I still can’t believe it.

Link Devi
While there’s great excitement about the discovery of the debris, it’s easy to forget that this is still a story about human tragedy.

Sound Up Family Member
So our emotion is always up and down, up and down you know?

Voice
For those left behind, Malaysian Airlines Flight MH370 still holds more questions than answers.

Sound Up Family Member
It’s really awhile, it’s over 500 days, and we are counting days also. And I don’t want that to be until the rest of my life.

Voice
The Malaysian government has been severely criticized for their handling of the tragedy, especially in the critical weeks directly after the incident. The lack of progress has led to any number of conspiracy theories surfacing in popular media.

Sound Up Low Ting Lai Malaysian Transport Minister
So whatever conspiracy theory, I think that it is not true. It’s better to listen to the expert, with very good foundation, very good basis to believe in.

Voice
Neels has been contacted by relatives of the victims of flight MH370, and says they all have one thing in common – a need for closure.

Sound Up Neels
You know the more I speak to these relatives, the more I just really hope that this piece, Liam’s piece, Blaine’s piece, all these pieces will really just provide some kind of answer, because these people are in dire need of an answer, of some kind of closure.

Sound Up Family Member
I don’t like to show this so much to people and I don’t want people to think we are asking for sympathy. No, I’m not looking for that. And they say they understand our feelings, but actually they don’t.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Two South Africans have recently found debris which could turn out to be from the missing Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 - could the finds finally bring closure to the families of the 239 victims?
metadata.Summary: In December 2015, Liam Lotter, an 18 year old South African, found a piece of aeroplane debris floating off the coast of Mozambique where he was on holiday with his family. Then in March this year Neels Kruger found another piece in Mossel Bay and has been sent to Australia for testing. These two parts brings the total possible finds to 4 pieces. If confirmed, could these be parts help solve the mystery that is Flight MH370?
metadata.Further information: Our story will recap the original incident with victims, the rescue teams and the all efforts to recover any of the wreckage. Both South African case studies have agreed to speak to us. We'll be speaking to experts in the aviation industry to be better understand what went wrong, and why in today's techno age we still don't know what happened to the 239 people aboard. Conspiracy theorist and self-proclaimed MH370 investigator Blaine Gibson has been around the world trying to locate the missing flight. Last year he found a confirmed piece (the second), also off of the coast of African - in Mozambique. We've approached him for an interview, if he does not return contact we've got his websites, video's and photo's of him conducting his investigations. He is one of many "conspiracy theorists" and has compiled a list of facts and questions. We do have footage of the man in the reunion islands who found a confirmed piece last year, he was the first to do so, and since then the investigations have primarily been focused on the South Indian Ocean. Lastly, we will be speaking to an expert to the South African weather services who can explain flo-patterns in the ocean and why the debris is landing on Southern Africa's shores. The South African Civil Aviation authority is providing us with general footage that can be used for the story, as well as an interview with an air traffic control expert.
